title: On the Origin and Evolution of Training-Inference Mismatch in LLM Reinforcement Learning

paper.title: On the Origin and Evolution of Training-Inference Mismatch in LLM Reinforcement Learning
paper.abstract:
Abstract On-policy reinforcement learning for large language models assumes that training responses are sampled from the current policy.
In practice, an inference engine samples the responses and a separate trainer computes the gradients, and the training-inference mismatch between the two makes the training data off-policy. The mismatch has two sources, the numerics of the engine and the stale weights of asynchronous sampling, and a correction that stabilizes training under one source can fail under the other. We ask which property of a mismatch source decides the correction it needs. Evaluating the trainer at the sampler’s weights splits each sampled-token error exactly into a numerical discrepancy of the engine and a policy lag of the trainer, and we follow both through training. The numerical discrepancy stays approximately constant, so it biases the updates by a nearly fixed amount, and centering the score at each prefix removes its leading bias. The policy lag is produced by the trainer’s own updates: the bias it leaves enters the next update, which enlarges the next lag and closes a feedback loop. Importance weighting cuts this loop only while the lag ratio stays concentrated, and on Qwen3-1.7B it fails at the step where the effective sample size of the ratio falls below one half. From this account we derive the discrepancy-lag correction (DLC), which centers the numerical discrepancy, clips the lag ratio against the sampler’s weights and resynchronizes the sampler when this effective sample size falls below one half. Under a stale sampler, DLC keeps the KL divergence from on-policy training within twice the KL between two independent on-policy trainings on Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B, and its resynchronization prevents collapses that the per-token corrections leave and that a KL measured on the sampler’s prefixes does not detect.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Reinforcement learning for language models ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2026a ; Zhou et al., 2026a ) typically runs two systems on the same weights. Inference engines such as vLLM ( Kwon et al., 2023 ; Zheng et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2026b ) sample the responses, and a trainer computes the policy gradient on them. The engine computes token probabilities with its own kernels and precision, so its distribution q q differs from the trainer’s distribution p p even at identical weights ( Yao et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025a ) , and low-precision samplers widen the gap. Asynchronous systems such as AReaL ( Fu et al., 2025 ) and PipelineRL ( Piché et al., 2025 ) add a second source, since the sampler keeps the weights of the last synchronization while the trainer moves on. Training on samples from q q with gradients of p p is therefore off-policy. We call the whole gap between q q and p p , from both sources, the training-inference mismatch . Prior work addresses this mismatch with three corrections ( Yao et al., 2025 ; Marek and Ryabinin, 2026 ; Schulman et al., 2017 ) : (1) truncated importance sampling weights each sampled token by the truncated ratio p / q p/q ; (2) score centering subtracts the sampler’s mean score at each prefix and thereby removes the drift, the part of the update that depends on the advantages only through their mean; (3) PPO clips the ratio of the trainer to a reference policy at each token. The outcome of these corrections depends on the source of the mismatch. Score centering keeps training stable with a quantized sampler and falls behind importance sampling with a stale one, while PPO trains under staleness and fails under quantization ( Marek and Ryabinin, 2026 ) . Under staleness alone the collapse of asynchronous GRPO scales with the product of staleness and learning rate ( Song et al., 2026 ) , and importance-weighted asynchronous training loses its effective sample size before it diverges ( Huang et al., 2026 ) . The behavior of a correction therefore depends jointly on the estimator and on the process that produces the mismatch. At a single prefix, however, the untruncated ratio and centering both remove the drift, so the source must act through what each correction leaves after the drift and through how that remainder evolves during training. The question is which property of a mismatch source decides the correction it needs. We trace the mismatch to its origin in the two layers of the system and follow its evolution during training. The infrastructure decides how far the sampler departs from the trainer, and the algorithm corrects what reaches the gradient. Once the infrastructure aligns sampling, reporting and token sequences, the mismatch reaches the algorithm as a numerical discrepancy and a policy lag, and the trainer’s log-probability at the sampler’s weights splits the sampled-token error exactly into these two terms, as Figure 1 illustrates. The numerical discrepancy originates in the engine and stays approximately fixed during training. The policy lag originates in the trainer’s own updates, the residual bias it leaves enters the next update, and the next update sets the next lag. Corrections of the policy lag therefore have to keep this loop from amplifying the update. Our contributions follow this account. ❶ Following the factorization of the importance ratio at the sampler’s weights ( Guan et al., 2026 ) , we split the sampled-token error exactly into the numerical discrepancy and the policy lag. After centering removes the drift, the remaining bias consists of a prefix, a continuation, a token and a tail term, which keep a fixed size for the numerical discrepancy and grow with the accumulated update for the policy lag. ❷ For the policy lag, the token and prefix terms enter the next update and close a loop, which locates the part of the known staleness bias ( Song et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) that survives centering. As a consequence, the excess update norm of score centering over importance sampling has a positive quadratic term in the product η ​ k \eta k of learning rate and step count. Ratio weighting removes the token term within its validity range, which ends where the effective sample size of the lag ratio falls below one half. On Qwen3-1.7B the heavy tail of the ratio brings this crossing to step 11, three steps before the Gaussian prediction, and importance sampling leaves the noise floor at that step. ❸ The discrepancy-lag correction (DLC) centers the numerical discrepancy, clips the lag ratio against the sampler’s weights ( Chang et al., 2026a ) and resynchronizes the sampler at the end of the validity range. Under a stale sampler DLC keeps the deviation from on-policy training within twice the noise floor on Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B, and on Qwen3-1.7B the resynchronization prevents the collapses that the clip alone leaves.

sections.heading: 2.1 Training-inference mismatch
sections.text: Table 1 lists the mismatch by the layer that corrects it. Once the infrastructure aligns sampling, reporting and token sequences, only the weight version and the engine numerics reach the algorithm, and only the weight version changes with the update. The other three rows of the infrastructure layer concern what the sampler reports and what the trainer receives. Top-p sampling and processed log-probabilities make the reported q q differ from the distribution that drew the token, so the sampler has to report the drawn distribution. Retokenization of the decoded text can change the token sequence, and passing token ids to the trainer keeps the sequence identical on both sides. Filtering responses by their reward and deferring long responses in partial rollouts make the composition of the batch depend on the outcome, and outcome-independent batching keeps the batch a sample of q q . These three mismatches vanish under the configuration of Section 3 , so the weight version and the engine numerics remain as the two sources that the algorithm has to correct. In the algorithm layer, the weight version gives the policy lag, which grows with the update, and decoupled PPO and M2PO weight the ratio of the trainer to the sampler’s weights, while VCPO scales the learning rate by the effective sample size. The engine numerics give the numerical discrepancy, which stays approximately fixed in training, and truncated importance sampling and score centering correct it at each sampled token. Zhong et al. (2026) isolate the numerical discrepancy against a bitwise-aligned reference engine, and Yu et al. For quantized samplers in synchronous training, AIS and QaRL weight the discrepancy factor separately from the PPO ratio ( Zhou et al., 2026b ; Gu et al., 2026 ) , and Chen et al. (2026) calibrate the clip range to the quantization noise. QeRL instead trains with a quantized sampler and uses its quantization noise for exploration ( Huang et al., 2025 ) . QUADS aligns the quantization errors of the sampler and the trainer for mixture-of-experts models in 4-bit floating point ( Zhuge et al., 2026 ) . Marek and Ryabinin (2026) trace the instability under mismatch to the drift, the term of the policy gradient that Section 3 defines, and remove it by subtracting the sampler’s mean score at each prefix. In their experiments the outcome of each correction depends on the mismatch source. With a quantized sampler, score centering alone trains best, and with a sampler synchronized every 64 steps, importance sampling with centering trains while score centering alone falls behind. PPO survives staleness and collapses under quantization and under synthetic weight noise. The authors attribute the stale case to the covariance that score centering takes under the sampler and the survival of PPO to a clip designed for ratios from policy movement. Our account places the sampler inside a training loop, since the sampler is a biased copy of the trainer that synchronizes back to it. Section 4 separates the part of the mismatch that moves with the trainer from the part that stays fixed, and Section 5 follows the remainder after centering for the moving part through training.

sections.heading: 2.2 Off-policy correction and staleness
sections.text: Truncated and clipped importance weights have a long history in off-policy reinforcement learning ( Ionides, 2008 ; Munos et al., 2016 ; Espeholt et al., 2018 ) , and ACER combines truncation with a bias-correction term over the full action set ( Wang et al., 2017 ) . Asynchronous systems bound the staleness and weight each token by its ratio to the logged rollout policy ( Fu et al., 2025 ; Piché et al., 2025 ; Noukhovitch et al., 2025 ) , decoupled PPO separates a proximal policy from the behavior policy ( Hilton et al., 2022 ) , and GSPO clips the ratio at the sequence level ( Zheng et al., 2025c ) . Guan et al. (2026) show that the importance ratio factors into a training-inference discrepancy and a policy staleness and that this factorization needs the trainer’s log-probabilities at the old weights. Song et al. (2026) trace the collapse of asynchronous GRPO to a staleness-induced update bias that positive feedback across synchronization periods sustains, and COPC couples the correction of the policy ratio with that of the advantage estimate ( Hu et al., 2026 ) . Adaptive schemes control the update through statistics of the ratio. For example, M2PO bounds the second moment of the importance weights ( Zheng et al., 2025a ) , VCPO scales the learning rate by the effective sample size ( Huang et al., 2026 ) , and Guan et al. (2026) reset the proximal reference when the share of unmasked tokens falls below 0.9. Other studies act on the update itself in three ways ( Chang et al., 2026b ) . GAC finds that successive gradients of asynchronous training stay aligned and projects the update off the stale-aligned direction ( Xu et al., 2026 ) , SAT shrinks one side of the PPO trust region with the log-ratio as a proxy for staleness ( Yang et al., 2026 ) , and GMC-GRPO caps the importance mass of each group and bounds the bias of trajectory-level weighted estimators ( He et al., 2026 ) . GAC, SAT and GMC-GRPO analyze the update without centering and do not separate the policy lag from the numerical discrepancy. The discrepancy-lag correction of Section 7 builds on the factorization of Guan et al. (2026) , gives each factor its own correction according to whether it enters the training loop and uses the second moment of the lag ratio to resynchronize the sampler’s weights.

sections.heading: 3.2 Mismatch sources and training
sections.text: The reference sampler runs vLLM in BF16 with CUDA graphs and yields on-policy training. The quantized sampler stores the weights in FP8 ( Micikevicius et al., 2022 ) with 128 × 128 128\times 128 blocks, quantizes the activations dynamically and keeps an FP8 KV cache. The stale sampler runs in BF16 and synchronizes every 64 steps, so within the 40 training steps it keeps the initial weights θ 0 \theta_{0} and the accumulated update is Δ = θ − θ 0 \Delta=\theta-\theta_{0} . The combined source quantizes the stale weights θ 0 \theta_{0} in the same way. The four samplers draw at temperature one without truncation and pass token ids to the trainer, so the sampling, reporting and sequence mismatches of Table 1 vanish. We train Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B ( Qwen Team, 2025 ) in non-thinking mode on Countdown with rewards ± 1 \pm 1 , 64 prompts with eight samples per step and SGD ( Chang et al., 2025 ) at learning rate 10 − 2 10^{-2} , and train each configuration three times for 40 steps. These short trainings, together with replay of the sampler on shared checkpoints, keep the measurements on trajectories that have not collapsed. The deviation of a trained model is its full-vocabulary KL to the on-policy model trained with the same configuration on fixed prefixes from θ 0 \theta_{0} , averaged over the three pairs and divided by the noise floor, the mean KL between two independently trained on-policy models. Test accuracy is measured on 64 Countdown problems outside the training set with eight samples each. Appendix A collects the notation.

sections.heading: 6.2 Reference policy of PPO
sections.text: The same derivation fixes the role of the PPO reference policy. With the reference at the sampler’s weights, the clipped ratio is e ℓ t e^{\ell_{t}} , so the clip bounds the token term as the importance sampling ratio does and leaves the numerical discrepancy outside the ratio as drift. With the reference at the trainer before each batch, the policy lag stays outside the ratio, and the clip bounds only the movement between the updates within a batch. Our PPO runs take four updates per batch, and PPO without clip takes the same updates with the clip removed. Under staleness, PPO with the batch reference deviates at least as far as PPO without clip, at 699 against 534 times the floor in Table 2 , while the sampler-weight reference of DLC stays at 1.9. Under quantization, PPO stays at the level of the policy gradient with one update per batch, so the clip removes the cost of the extra updates and leaves the drift of the numerical discrepancy. Marek and Ryabinin (2026) attribute this asymmetry to a clip designed for ratios that come from policy movement, and Chen et al. (2026) observe that quantization noise in the ratio pushes negative-advantage tokens outside the clip range. The position of the reference policy therefore accounts for the asymmetry. With the sampler’s weights as reference, the policy lag lies inside the ratio of PPO and the numerical discrepancy outside it, so the clip contains the lag under staleness and leaves the drift of the discrepancy under quantization. Our runs test the batch reference directly and the sampler reference through DLC, which shares its clipped ratio.

The collapses without resynchronization coincide with a jump of the trainer’s mass on tokens to which θ 0 \theta_{0} gives probability below 10 − 3 10^{-3} , and this mass stays low under DLC (d). Test accuracy measures the trainer on its own responses and broadly orders the corrections as the deviation does. On Qwen3-0.6B under staleness, DLC and importance sampling with centering end at 31.7% and 32.0% at step 40, against 46.5% for on-policy training and 12.2% for score centering. Each of these checkpoints scores at or above θ 0 \theta_{0} , so the gap reflects accuracy that the runs have not yet reached. On Qwen3-1.7B the three DLC models end at 51.9% on average against 57.6% for on-policy training, each within 7 percentage points of its on-policy counterpart in panel c. Importance sampling with resynchronization averages 36.6%, since one of its runs collapses. Appendix C extends the comparison to Qwen3-8B, where DLC and importance sampling with centering stay within about three times the floor while score centering reaches 89 times, and to continuous asynchrony on Qwen3-1.7B, where DLC ends at 1.2 times the floor.

sections.heading: 7.3 Mass off the support of the initial policy
sections.text: DLC without resynchronization keeps the clip and the centering and shows why DLC needs the resynchronization. On Qwen3-1.7B two of its three runs fall below the accuracy of θ 0 \theta_{0} by step 40 and produce answers of about 26 tokens, and the collapsed run of importance sampling with resynchronization writes responses up to the length limit. The deviation of these runs, computed on the sampler’s prefixes, stays at the floor. Centering, ratio weighting and clipping act on the tokens that the sampler draws, so a shift toward tokens that the stale sampler rarely draws remains outside the reach of these three corrections. The trainer’s own responses measure such a shift through their sequence KL to θ 0 \theta_{0} , 𝔼 p θ ​ [ ∑ t log ⁡ p θ ​ ( y t ∣ h t ) − log ⁡ p θ 0 ​ ( y t ∣ h t ) ] \mathbb{E}_{p_{\theta}}\big[\sum_{t}\log p_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid h_{t})-\log p_{\theta_{0}}(y_{t}\mid h_{t})\big] , and through the off-support share of this KL, the fraction on tokens with p θ 0 ​ ( y t ) < 10 − 3 p_{\theta_{0}}(y_{t})<10^{-3} . At the two collapses of DLC without resynchronization the off-support share reaches about 90%, against at most 14% before them, as panel d of Figure 5 shows. Across the Qwen3-1.7B checkpoints the off-support share ranks the drop below θ 0 \theta_{0} at a Spearman correlation of 0.80, above the 0.74 of the deviation. On the sampler’s prefixes, the next-token KL of the collapsed runs stays within the range of the runs that keep learning. The shift therefore starts on prefixes that the stale sampler does not reach. Resynchronization moves the sampler and the reference of the clip to the trainer’s weights, so the trainer’s responses become the sampler’s responses again. Under DLC the off-support share stays at or below 11% through step 40, and the three runs stay above the accuracy of θ 0 \theta_{0} .

sections.heading: 8 Conclusion
sections.text: Training-inference mismatch reaches the gradient as two components with different dynamics. The numerical discrepancy of the engine stays approximately fixed during training, so removing its drift suffices. The policy lag comes from the trainer’s own updates and feeds back through the residual bias of centering into later updates, and ratio weighting cuts this loop only until the effective sample size of the lag ratio falls below one half. DLC follows this account: it centers the discrepancy, clips the lag ratio and resynchronizes the sampler at that crossing, which keeps a stale sampler within twice the noise floor and prevents the collapses that the off-support share of the trainer’s own responses reveals.

sections.heading: Reproducibility
sections.text: Appendix B lists the training configuration, the mismatch sources and the measurement protocol, and Appendix L gives the loss of DLC. The trainings run in verl with vLLM samplers, three per configuration on Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B, and the offline measurements use fixed checkpoints and fixed probe prefixes.

In practice, an inference engine samples the responses and a separate trainer computes the gradients, and the training-inference mismatch between the two makes the training data off-policy. The mismatch has two sources, the numerics of the engine and the stale weights of asynchronous sampling, and a correction that stabilizes training under one source can fail under the other. We ask which property of a mismatch source decides the correction it needs. Evaluating the trainer at the sampler’s weights splits each sampled-token error exactly into a numerical discrepancy of the engine and a policy lag of the trainer, and we follow both through training. The numerical discrepancy stays approximately constant, so it biases the updates by a nearly fixed amount, and centering the score at each prefix removes its leading bias. The policy lag is produced by the trainer’s own updates: the bias it leaves enters the next update, which enlarges the next lag and closes a feedback loop. Importance weighting cuts this loop only while the lag ratio stays concentrated, and on Qwen3-1.7B it fails at the step where the effective sample size of the ratio falls below one half. From this account we derive the discrepancy-lag correction (DLC), which centers the numerical discrepancy, clips the lag ratio against the sampler’s weights and resynchronizes the sampler when this effective sample size falls below one half. Under a stale sampler, DLC keeps the KL divergence from on-policy training within twice the KL between two independent on-policy trainings on Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B, and its resynchronization prevents collapses that the per-token corrections leave and that a KL measured on the sampler’s prefixes does not detect. † † footnotetext: ∗ Equal contribution. Correspondence: yul@gwu.edu , yufa.zhou@duke.edu , tlan@gwu.edu . (a) Origin, evolution and correction of the mismatch Figure 1: Origin of the training-inference mismatch and the correction built on it. The trainer’s forward pass at the sampler’s weights splits the mismatch exactly into the numerical discrepancy and the policy lag, and the gradient estimator receives a constant offset from the first and a growing lag ratio from the second. DLC subtracts the offset, clips the lag ratio inside the loop through the update and resynchronizes the sampler when the effective sample size of the lag ratio falls below one half (a) . Under a stale sampler, DLC keeps Qwen3-1.7B at the noise floor through step 40, while importance sampling leaves the floor once its effective sample size falls below one half at step 11 (b) . The three DLC trainings resynchronize the sampler when the effective sample size of their lag ratio falls below one half, and the effective sample size of importance sampling stays below one half after step 11 (c) . 1 Introduction Reinforcement learning for language models ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2026a ; Zhou et al., 2026a ) typically runs two systems on the same weights. Inference engines such as vLLM ( Kwon et al., 2023 ; Zheng et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2026b ) sample the responses, and a trainer computes the policy gradient on them. The engine computes token probabilities with its own kernels and precision, so its distribution q q differs from the trainer’s distribution p p even at identical weights ( Yao et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025a ) , and low-precision samplers widen the gap. Asynchronous systems such as AReaL ( Fu et al., 2025 ) and PipelineRL ( Piché et al., 2025 ) add a second source, since the sampler keeps the weights of the last synchronization while the trainer moves on. Training on samples from q q with gradients of p p is therefore off-policy. We call the whole gap between q q and p p , from both sources, the training-inference mismatch . Prior work addresses this mismatch with three corrections ( Yao et al., 2025 ; Marek and Ryabinin, 2026 ; Schulman et al., 2017 ) : (1) truncated importance sampling weights each sampled token by the truncated ratio p / q p/q ; (2) score centering subtracts the sampler’s mean score at each prefix and thereby removes the drift, the part of the update that depends on the advantages only through their mean; (3) PPO clips the ratio of the trainer to a reference policy at each token. The outcome of these corrections depends on the source of the mismatch. Score centering keeps training stable with a quantized sampler and falls behind importance sampling with a stale one, while PPO trains under staleness and fails under quantization ( Marek and Ryabinin, 2026 ) . Under staleness alone the collapse of asynchronous GRPO scales with the product of staleness and learning rate ( Song et al., 2026 ) , and importance-weighted asynchronous training loses its effective sample size before it diverges ( Huang et al., 2026 ) . The behavior of a correction therefore depends jointly on the estimator and on the process that produces the mismatch. At a single prefix, however, the untruncated ratio and centering both remove the drift, so the source must act through what each correction leaves after the drift and through how that remainder evolves during training. The question is which property of a mismatch source decides the correction it needs. We trace the mismatch to its origin in the two layers of the system and follow its evolution during training. The infrastructure decides how far the sampler departs from the trainer, and the algorithm corrects what reaches the gradient. Once the infrastructure aligns sampling, reporting and token sequences, the mismatch reaches the algorithm as a numerical discrepancy and a policy lag, and the trainer’s log-probability at the sampler’s weights splits the sampled-token error exactly into these two terms, as Figure 1 illustrates. The numerical discrepancy originates in the engine and stays approximately fixed during training. The policy lag originates in the trainer’s own updates, the residual bias it leaves enters the next update, and the next update sets the next lag. Corrections of the policy lag therefore have to keep this loop from amplifying the update. Our contributions follow this account. ❶ Following the factorization of the importance ratio at the sampler’s weights ( Guan et al., 2026 ) , we split the sampled-token error exactly into the numerical discrepancy and the policy lag. After centering removes the drift, the remaining bias consists of a prefix, a continuation, a token and a tail term, which keep a fixed size for the numerical discrepancy and grow with the accumulated update for the policy lag. ❷ For the policy lag, the token and prefix terms enter the next update and close a loop, which locates the part of the known staleness bias ( Song et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) that survives centering. As a consequence, the excess update norm of score centering over importance sampling has a positive quadratic term in the product η ​ k \eta k of learning rate and step count. Ratio weighting removes the token term within its validity range, which ends where the effective sample size of the lag ratio falls below one half. On Qwen3-1.7B the heavy tail of the ratio brings this crossing to step 11, three steps before the Gaussian prediction, and importance sampling leaves the noise floor at that step. ❸ The discrepancy-lag correction (DLC) centers the numerical discrepancy, clips the lag ratio against the sampler’s weights ( Chang et al., 2026a ) and resynchronizes the sampler at the end of the validity range. Under a stale sampler DLC keeps the deviation from on-policy training within twice the noise floor on Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B, and on Qwen3-1.7B the resynchronization prevents the collapses that the clip alone leaves. 2 Background 2.1 Training-inference mismatch Table 1 lists the mismatch by the layer that corrects it. Once the infrastructure aligns sampling, reporting and token sequences, only the weight version and the engine numerics reach the algorithm, and only the weight version changes with the update. The other three rows of the infrastructure layer concern what the sampler reports and what the trainer receives. Top-p sampling and processed log-probabilities make the reported q q differ from the distribution that drew the token, so the sampler has to report the drawn distribution. Retokenization of the decoded text can change the token sequence, and passing token ids to the trainer keeps the sequence identical on both sides. Filtering responses by their reward and deferring long responses in partial rollouts make the composition of the batch depend on the outcome, and outcome-independent batching keeps the batch a sample of q q . These three mismatches vanish under the configuration of Section 3 , so the weight version and the engine numerics remain as the two sources that the algorithm has to correct. In the algorithm layer, the weight version gives the policy lag, which grows with the update, and decoupled PPO and M2PO weight the ratio of the trainer to the sampler’s weights, while VCPO scales the learning rate by the effective sample size. The engine numerics give the numerical discrepancy, which stays approximately fixed in training, and truncated importance sampling and score centering correct it at each sampled token. (2025) reported that vLLM and FSDP give different token probabilities at identical weights and introduced truncated importance sampling, and Liu et al. (2025a) traced the gap to engine numerics, quantization and kernels and proposed sequence-level variants. Zheng et al. (2025b) showed that the token-level objective approximates the sequence-level one only when both the numerical gap and the staleness are small. Engineering work reduces the numerical discrepancy through batch-invariant kernels ( He and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025 ) , deterministic inference across tensor-parallel sizes ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) , FP16 training ( Qi et al., 2025 ) , an FP32 language-model head ( MiniMax, 2025 ) and router replay for mixture-of-experts models ( Ma et al., 2025 ) . Zhong et al. (2026) isolate the numerical discrepancy against a bitwise-aligned reference engine, and Yu et al. (2026) model it as a displacement of the logits and calibrate the importance weight accordingly. For quantized samplers in synchronous training, AIS and QaRL weight the discrepancy factor separately from the PPO ratio ( Zhou et al., 2026b ; Gu et al., 2026 ) , and Chen et al. (2026) calibrate the clip range to the quantization noise. QeRL instead trains with a quantized sampler and uses its quantization noise for exploration ( Huang et al., 2025 ) . QUADS aligns the quantization errors of the sampler and the trainer for mixture-of-experts models in 4-bit floating point ( Zhuge et al., 2026 ) . Marek and Ryabinin (2026) trace the instability under mismatch to the drift, the term of the policy gradient that Section 3 defines, and remove it by subtracting the sampler’s mean score at each prefix. In their experiments the outcome of each correction depends on the mismatch source. With a quantized sampler, score centering alone trains best, and with a sampler synchronized every 64 steps, importance sampling with centering trains while score centering alone falls behind. PPO survives staleness and collapses under quantization and under synthetic weight noise. The authors attribute the stale case to the covariance that score centering takes under the sampler and the survival of PPO to a clip designed for ratios from policy movement. Our account places the sampler inside a training loop, since the sampler is a biased copy of the trainer that synchronizes back to it. Section 4 separates the part of the mismatch that moves with the trainer from the part that stays fixed, and Section 5 follows the remainder after centering for the moving part through training. 2.2 Off-policy correction and staleness Truncated and clipped importance weights have a long history in off-policy reinforcement learning ( Ionides, 2008 ; Munos et al., 2016 ; Espeholt et al., 2018 ) , and ACER combines truncation with a bias-correction term over the full action set ( Wang et al., 2017 ) . Asynchronous systems bound the staleness and weight each token by its ratio to the logged rollout policy ( Fu et al., 2025 ; Piché et al., 2025 ; Noukhovitch et al., 2025 ) , decoupled PPO separates a proximal policy from the behavior policy ( Hilton et al., 2022 ) , and GSPO clips the ratio at the sequence level ( Zheng et al., 2025c ) . Guan et al. (2026) show that the importance ratio factors into a training-inference discrepancy and a policy staleness and that this factorization needs the trainer’s log-probabilities at the old weights. Song et al. (2026) trace the collapse of asynchronous GRPO to a staleness-induced update bias that positive feedback across synchronization periods sustains, and COPC couples the correction of the policy ratio with that of the advantage estimate ( Hu et al., 2026 ) . Adaptive schemes control the update through statistics of the ratio. For example, M2PO bounds the second moment of the importance weights ( Zheng et al., 2025a ) , VCPO scales the learning rate by the effective sample size ( Huang et al., 2026 ) , and Guan et al. (2026) reset the proximal reference when the share of unmasked tokens falls below 0.9. Other studies act on the update itself in three ways ( Chang et al., 2026b ) . GAC finds that successive gradients of asynchronous training stay aligned and projects the update off the stale-aligned direction ( Xu et al., 2026 ) , SAT shrinks one side of the PPO trust region with the log-ratio as a proxy for staleness ( Yang et al., 2026 ) , and GMC-GRPO caps the importance mass of each group and bounds the bias of trajectory-level weighted estimators ( He et al., 2026 ) . GAC, SAT and GMC-GRPO analyze the update without centering and do not separate the policy lag from the numerical discrepancy. The numerical discrepancy of the engine stays approximately fixed during training, so removing its drift suffices. The policy lag comes from the trainer’s own updates and feeds back through the residual bias of centering into later updates, and ratio weighting cuts this loop only until the effective sample size of the lag ratio falls below one half. DLC follows this account: it centers the discrepancy, clips the lag ratio and resynchronizes the sampler at that crossing, which keeps a stale sampler within twice the noise floor and prevents the collapses that the off-support share of the trainer’s own responses reveals.
